title: AI Infrastructure Earnings Week Tests Whether the Capex Boom Is Justified
summary: Results from CoreWeave, Supermicro and Applied Materials this week functioned as a live referendum on the AI spending debate that has hung over markets since hyperscalers guided toward $775-800 billion of 2026 capital expenditure. The numbers matter less as a one-week earnings beat than as a test of whether real demand is catching up with the scale of investment, after months of analysts and rating agencies warning that spending is outrunning cash flow.
context:
- Moody's warned in July that hyperscalers have roughly $662 billion in data-centre lease commitments signed but not yet commenced, obligations that sit off balance sheet under GAAP's lease-commencement rules and so do not show up in the capex figures investors typically scrutinise.

- Total AI-related lease commitments across the group have ballooned toward $1.2 trillion, with projected 2026 capex tracking near $785 billion and 2027 toward $1 trillion, a trajectory Moody's says is eroding free cash flow and pressuring credit quality at firms including Amazon, Meta and Alphabet.

- The scepticism has already shown up in share prices: Alphabet fell around 7% after reporting its first negative free cash flow quarter since its 2004 IPO despite 82% growth in cloud revenue, and S&P downgraded Oracle's credit rating in July, citing surging capex and customer concentration.

- Against that backdrop, CoreWeave's forecast of $3.45-3.6 billion in third-quarter sales plus a swelling order backlog, and strong numbers from server maker Supermicro, sent AI infrastructure stocks broadly higher, easing without eliminating concern that spending is outrunning revenue.

- Applied Materials' comparatively muted share reaction despite solid earnings suggests the market is now discriminating between AI demand signals, such as chips, servers and cloud compute, and equipment suppliers more exposed to the broader semiconductor cycle, rather than treating every AI-adjacent name as a uniform bet.

title: Gold's Push Toward $4,500 Reflects a Deeper Shift Away From the Dollar
summary: Gold's climb back above $4,400 an ounce this week is best understood not as a simple safe-haven trade but as the visible edge of a structural shift in how central banks hold their reserves. The move matters because it is being driven less by day-to-day trading sentiment than by sustained official-sector buying and a multi-year push by major emerging economies to reduce their reliance on the dollar.
context:
- Central banks, led by China, India and Turkey, bought a record 289 tonnes of gold in the second quarter of 2026 alone, part of a multi-year drive by emerging-market reserve managers to diversify away from dollar-denominated assets.

- Analysts attribute roughly 30-35% of gold's price appreciation this cycle directly to official-sector buying, a source of demand that does not depend on retail or speculative positioning and has persisted through gold's sharp swings over the past 18 months.

- The path has not been linear: gold surged to a record near $5,600 an ounce in January before slumping more than 20% in its worst quarter since 2013, only to rebound back through $4,400 by mid-August, underlining how volatile the adjustment to reduced dollar reliance has been.

- The rally has also been reinforced by monetary policy: as markets price a greater chance the Federal Reserve holds rates or cuts rather than resumes hiking, following the shock July payrolls contraction, expected real yields have fallen, lowering the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset like gold.

- China's accumulation is tied to its longer-term ambition to internationalise the renminbi and reduce dependence on the dollar-based settlement system, meaning the buying reflects strategic reserve diversification as much as any near-term trading view.

title: Berkshire's Numbers Show What Investing Looks Like After Buffett
summary: Berkshire Hathaway's latest quarter offered the clearest evidence yet of how Greg Abel intends to run the conglomerate now that he has succeeded Warren Buffett as chief executive. The results matter less for the headline earnings jump than for what they reveal about a shift in capital allocation, from years of net stock selling and cash hoarding toward renewed buying, at the firm long defined by Buffett's own instincts.
context:
- Greg Abel took over as Berkshire's chief executive at the start of 2026, ending Warren Buffett's six-decade run atop the conglomerate; Buffett remains chairman, but this quarter was the clearest test yet of how Abel intends to deploy the firm's famous cash pile.

- Berkshire had spent much of the prior two years selling far more stock than it bought, building cash reserves to record levels; this quarter marked a reversal, with the firm becoming a net buyer of equities for the first time in that stretch, purchasing roughly $20 billion more stock than it sold.

- Operating earnings rose 16% in the quarter as strength in Berkshire's energy, railroad and manufacturing units offset softer results from its insurance operations, a diversification that has long underpinned the conglomerate's resilience through different rate and market cycles.

- Investment gains of roughly $10.9 billion, aided by a rebound in equity markets, more than doubled net income quarter-on-quarter; Berkshire has cautioned for years that such mark-to-market gains reflect accounting rules rather than underlying operating performance.

- Around $4.5 billion of share buybacks in the quarter, alongside the return to net equity purchases, signals that Abel currently sees Berkshire's own stock and selected public equities as more attractively priced than sitting on cash, an early data point on how the post-Buffett capital allocation approach may differ in emphasis from his predecessor's famously patient style.
